## Data and training/test split

We use the same data-building code as Milestone 2: weekly counts of NFL injury-report
records for Weeks 1–17 of the 2016–2025 regular seasons, excluding resting-player reports
and records with no primary injury listed. Following our evaluation plan, the 2016–2024
seasons (`time` 1–153) form the training set and the 2025 season (`time` 154–170, one full
17-week forecast horizon) is the test set.

```{r}
#| label: building_data

library(nflreadr)
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)

# Load NFL injury reports from 2016–2025
injuries <- load_injuries(2016:2025)

# Create weekly injury-report counts
weekly_injuries <- injuries |>
  filter(week %in% 1:17) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(report_primary_injury),
    report_primary_injury != "Not injury related - resting player"
  ) |>
  group_by(season, week) |>
  summarise(
    injury_reports = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(season, week) |>
  mutate(
    time = (season - 2016) * 17 + week,
    week_label = paste0(season, " W", week)
  ) |>
  as_tsibble(index = time)

# Training set: 2016–2024 seasons; test set: 2025 season
train <- weekly_injuries |> filter(time <= 153)
test  <- weekly_injuries |> filter(time > 153)
```

### A note on the seasonal period

NFL regular-season weeks are not evenly spaced on the calendar: each season is followed by
roughly 35 weeks with no games. A date-based index (such as `yearweek`) would leave large
gaps in the series every off-season. We therefore index the series with a consecutive integer
`time` (1–170), so that Week 1 of one season directly follows Week 17 of the previous season.

The cost of this choice is that an integer index carries no calendar information, so fable
and feasts cannot infer the seasonal period on their own. `gg_season()` and `gg_subseries()`
fail on this index (they convert the period into calendar time), and an automatic `ETS()`
with no period specified silently fits a non-seasonal model. To avoid this, every model
below states the seasonal period of 17 weeks explicitly (`lag(17)`, `season(period = 17)`,
`PDQ(period = 17)`), and we built the seasonal plots by hand with ggplot. The plot below is
our stand-in for `gg_subseries()`: one panel per week of the season, with the blue line
showing that week's average across seasons.

```{r}
#| label: fig-subseries
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4

weekly_injuries |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(week) |>
  mutate(week_mean = mean(injury_reports)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = season, y = injury_reports)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = week_mean), color = "blue") +
  facet_wrap(~ week, nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2016, 2025)) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Subseries of NFL Injury Reports (Weeks 1–17)",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Number of Injury Reports"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, size = 7))
```

Week 1 is far below every other week in every season, and Weeks 2–17 sit at a similar level.
Within each week, counts move around from season to season without a clear upward or
downward trend.

## Predict first

Milestone 2 shows a strong, stable week-of-season pattern (seasonal strength 0.68, with a
low Week 1) and no long-run trend after 2016. We therefore expect a model that estimates a
smooth seasonal profile from many seasons to beat all four benchmarks. This could be ETS with
an additive seasonal component or a regression on week dummies. We expect the seasonal naive
method to come close but lose, because it copies only last season's noisy values. We expect
NAIVE and drift to do worst, because they cannot reproduce the Week 1 drop.

## Model fitting

We fit seven models to the training set: four benchmarks, ETS, ARIMA and a regression
model. Each model that uses seasonality is given the 17-week seasonal period explicitly.

```{r}
#| label: fit-models

fit <- train |>
  model(
    mean   = MEAN(injury_reports),
    naive  = NAIVE(injury_reports),
    snaive = SNAIVE(injury_reports ~ lag(17)),
    drift  = RW(injury_reports ~ drift()),
    ets    = ETS(injury_reports ~ season(period = 17)),
    arima  = ARIMA(injury_reports ~ PDQ(period = 17)),
    tslm   = TSLM(injury_reports ~ trend() + season(period = 17))
  )
```

### Benchmarks

- MEAN forecasts every future week as the average of all training weeks.
- NAIVE forecasts every future week as the last observed value (Week 17 of 2024).
- SNAIVE forecasts each week of 2025 as the value from the same week of 2024.
- RW with drift extends a straight line from the first to the last observation.

Only SNAIVE can reproduce the low Week 1, so we expect it to be the strongest benchmark.

### Exponential smoothing

```{r}
#| label: ets-report

fit |> select(ets)

fit |>
  select(ets) |>
  tidy() |>
  filter(term %in% c("alpha", "beta", "gamma", "phi"))
```

Automatic selection chose ETS(M,Ad,A):

- Error (M), multiplicative: the size of the random week-to-week variation is
  proportional to the level of the series.
- Trend (Ad), additive damped: the model allows a trend, but it flattens out
  (φ ≈ 0.93). The initial slope is negative, which reflects the drop from the high
  2016 season (average ≈ 176 reports per week) to roughly 140–150 in later seasons. Because the
  trend is damped, the model does not project that decline forward.
- Season (A), additive, period 17: each week of the season gets a fixed number of reports
  above or below the level. The Week 1 effect is about −58 reports. Weeks 2–17 lie
  mostly within ±20 of the level.

All three smoothing parameters (α, β, γ) are close to zero. This means the level, trend and
seasonal pattern hardly change over time. In effect, the model fits one fixed season shape
to all nine training seasons.

### ARIMA

Following FPP3 §9.1 and §9.5, we first use `unitroot_nsdiffs` to decide whether a
seasonal difference is needed. We then apply it and use the KPSS test and `unitroot_ndiffs`
on the seasonally differenced series to decide whether a further first difference is needed.

```{r}
#| label: unitroot

# Seasonal differences needed?
train |> features(injury_reports, unitroot_nsdiffs, .period = 17)

# KPSS test and first differences needed, after a seasonal difference
train |>
  mutate(diff_injuries = difference(injury_reports, lag = 17)) |>
  features(diff_injuries, list(unitroot_kpss, unitroot_ndiffs))
```

`unitroot_nsdiffs` suggests one seasonal difference (lag 17), because the seasonal
strength is high. After seasonal differencing, the KPSS test rejects stationarity at the 5%
level (p ≈ 0.02), and `unitroot_ndiffs` suggests one further first difference. Milestone 2
also found that a second difference produces strongly negative autocorrelation (−0.59), so
more than one first difference would be too many.

```{r}
#| label: arima-report

fit |> select(arima) |> report()
```

Automatic selection chose ARIMA(1,1,1)(2,1,0)[17]. `ARIMA()` chooses the differencing
with the same unit-root tests shown above (D = 1, d = 1). It then chooses the AR and MA orders
by minimizing AICc. The model has one non-seasonal AR term, one non-seasonal MA term, and two
seasonal AR terms. In words: the model forecasts each week
from changes relative to the same week last season, corrected by recent weeks' changes
and by the seasonal changes of the previous two seasons.

### Regression

Our data have no outside predictor series, so the regression model is a TSLM with a linear
trend and 16 week-of-season dummy variables:

$$
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{j=2}^{17} \gamma_j \, d_{j,t} + \varepsilon_t ,
$$

where $d_{j,t} = 1$ if observation $t$ falls in Week $j$. All future values of the
predictors (the time index and the week number) are known in advance, so this model has no
ex-ante forecasting problem. If we later add a real predictor, such as the number of games played
on short rest, we would need forecasts of that predictor (ex-ante). Otherwise we could only
report ex-post accuracy using its observed values (FPP3 §7.6).

## Forecast accuracy

### Test set (2025 season)

```{r}
#| label: fig-test-forecasts
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

fc <- fit |> forecast(h = 17)

fc |>
  filter(.model %in% c("snaive", "ets", "arima", "tslm")) |>
  autoplot(weekly_injuries |> filter(time > 119), level = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Forecasts of the 2025 Season vs. Actual Injury Reports",
    x = "Time (consecutive NFL week, 2023–2025 shown)",
    y = "Number of Injury Reports",
    color = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: accuracy-test

acc_measures <- list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE, MASE = MASE, CRPS = CRPS)

acc_test <- accuracy(fc, weekly_injuries, measures = acc_measures, .period = 17) |>
  select(-.type)
```

We compute RMSE, MAE, MASE and CRPS for each model. MASE is scaled by the seasonal naive
errors on the training data, using the 17-week period.

### Time series cross-validation

The single 2025 season could be unrepresentative, so we also use the expanding-window
cross-validation from our evaluation plan. The first training set is the first five seasons
(85 weeks), and each fold adds one season. Each fold forecasts the next 17 weeks, which gives
five forecast origins with training sets ending in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024.

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation

cv_data <- weekly_injuries |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 85, .step = 17) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id))   # drop the last fold, which has no future data to test on

cv_fit <- cv_data |>
  model(
    mean   = MEAN(injury_reports),
    naive  = NAIVE(injury_reports),
    snaive = SNAIVE(injury_reports ~ lag(17)),
    drift  = RW(injury_reports ~ drift()),
    ets    = ETS(injury_reports ~ season(period = 17)),
    arima  = ARIMA(injury_reports ~ PDQ(period = 17)),
    tslm   = TSLM(injury_reports ~ trend() + season(period = 17))
  )

cv_fc <- cv_fit |> forecast(h = 17)

acc_cv <- accuracy(cv_fc, weekly_injuries, measures = acc_measures, .period = 17) |>
  select(-.type)
```

### Accuracy comparison

```{r}
#| label: accuracy-table

# Accuracy on the 2025 test season and averaged over five CV folds (lower is better)
left_join(acc_test, acc_cv, by = ".model", suffix = c("_test", "_cv")) |>
  arrange(RMSE_cv) |>
  rename(Model = .model) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  print(width = Inf)
```

The table above shows accuracy on the 2025 test season (`_test`) and averaged over the five
cross-validation folds (`_cv`); lower is better. Our leading model is the seasonal naive
method (SNAIVE). On the 2025 test season it has the lowest value on all four measures, with an
RMSE of 18.9 compared with 21.0 for the next-best model, ETS. In cross-validation it again has
the lowest RMSE and CRPS. The regression model is a close second and essentially ties SNAIVE
on MAE and MASE. ETS and ARIMA beat the MEAN, NAIVE and drift benchmarks, but not SNAIVE.
NAIVE and drift are by far the worst, because they forecast a high value for Week 1. Since
ETS, ARIMA and the regression model do not beat the seasonal naive benchmark, none of them is
yet worth using in its place.

This result contradicts our prediction. Our interpretation is that the week-of-season shape
is the only part of the series that can be forecast reliably. Once a model captures the
Week 1 drop, most of the remaining variation is noise (Milestone 2 found a spectral entropy of
0.86). The extra parameters in ETS and ARIMA therefore add complexity without adding accuracy.
These models are also pulled upward by the unusually high 2016 season, which SNAIVE ignores
because it uses only the most recent season.

## Residual diagnostics for the leading model

```{r}
#| label: fig-snaive-resid
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

fit |>
  select(snaive) |>
  gg_tsresiduals(lag_max = 51) +
  labs(title = "Residuals of the Seasonal Naive Model (training data)")
```

```{r}
#| label: ljung-box

# Ljung-Box with lag = 2 x seasonal period; SNAIVE estimates no parameters (dof = 0)
fit |>
  select(snaive) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 34, dof = 0)

# For comparison: the ARIMA model (4 estimated coefficients)
fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 34, dof = 4)
```

The SNAIVE residuals are the season-over-season changes in each week's count (this season's
Week k minus last season's Week k). The model is unbiased overall: the residuals center
near zero and show no trend. However, they come in runs. For example, the first season of
residuals (2017 minus 2016) is almost entirely negative, reflecting the drop after the
unusually high 2016 season. Other seasons sit mostly above or mostly below zero.

The ACF confirms this. Autocorrelations at lags 1–3 are clearly positive (about 0.43 at
lag 1), so a week whose count is above last season's tends to be followed by more such weeks.
In other words, whole seasons shift up or down in level. There is also a negative spike at
lag 17 (about −0.32), which is typical of a seasonal-difference model: an unusually high week
this season makes next season's residual for that week negative. The Ljung–Box test
(lag 34, p < 0.001) strongly rejects white noise, so SNAIVE leaves usable structure in the
residuals, mainly the season-level shifts. The histogram is roughly symmetric and
bell-shaped, so normal prediction intervals are reasonable. However, the residuals are large
(mostly within ±40 reports), so the intervals will be wide.

The second Ljung–Box test above is for the ARIMA model, whose residuals pass (p ≈ 0.11).
ARIMA therefore captures the autocorrelation in the training data better than SNAIVE, yet
SNAIVE forecasts the 2025 season more accurately. The forecast plot shows where ARIMA goes
wrong: its forecasts are too high for most of Weeks 2–8. We return to this tension below.

## Status and open questions

(a) Who led each part

- Data import and test/CV setup: Thomas
- Benchmarks and ETS: Logan
- ARIMA and unit-root tests: Thomas
- Regression, accuracy table and diagnostics: Logan
- Writing and editing: Eli

(b) The problem we are most stuck on

Our main difficulty is the time index. We index the series by consecutive NFL week rather
than by calendar date, which avoids a 35-week gap every off-season. The drawback is that
fable and feasts cannot detect the 17-week season on their own. As a result, `gg_season()`
and `gg_subseries()` fail, and `ETS()` fits a non-seasonal model unless the period is given.
We tried converting the index to fake daily dates. The plots then ran, but they treated each
7-day block as a season, which is wrong. Our current solution is to specify `period = 17` in
every model and to draw the seasonal plots directly with ggplot. We would appreciate feedback
on whether this is an acceptable approach.

(c) What we plan to try before the final report

SNAIVE forecasts best even though its residuals are autocorrelated, while ARIMA passes the
Ljung–Box test but forecasts worse. We suspect the unusually high 2016 season and overfitting
of noise are responsible. To test this, we plan to:

- Repeat the comparison without the 2016 season, or with a 2016 level-shift dummy, to see
  whether ETS, ARIMA and the regression model then outperform SNAIVE.
- Fit a dynamic regression model (week dummies with ARIMA errors) and a simpler seasonal
  structure: a Week 1 dummy with a common level for Weeks 2–17.
- Examine era effects, including the 2020 COVID season and the move to an 18-week schedule
  in 2021 (we currently keep Weeks 1–17 only).
- Check whether a log or Box–Cox transformation improves the prediction intervals.
- Re-fit the final model on all ten seasons and produce 2026 forecasts with 80% and 95%
  prediction intervals.
